title: Logically Augmented Quantum LDPC Codes: Construction and Hierarchical Decoding
authors: Sheida Rabeti, Ayushi Shirke, Ivana Dimitrova, Hessam Mahdavifar
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07062v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a joint framework for constructing and decoding Logically Augmented (LA) quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. This is motivated by the need for flexible coding rates and adaptive error protection while preserving block length and code structure. On the construction side, we use an auxiliary \textit{Logical Protection Code (LPC)} to impose additional stabilizer constraints on selected logical qubits of a \textit{primary} code. On the decoding side, the proposed decoder uses the LPC syndrome to generate logical error hypotheses and condition belief propagation (BP) on each hypothesis. The proposed \textit{Hierarchical Logical List Decoder (HLLD)} is invoked only when the initial BP decoder for primary code fails to converge. It then selects the correction with the smallest Hamming weight among the syndrome-consistent candidates produced by hypothesis-conditioned BP runs.
  For numerical evaluation, we focus on short repetition LPCs, which provide a flexible means of trading rate for additional error protection. Each LPC syndrome admits exactly two logical error hypotheses, irrespective of repetition length, which enables HLLD to explore both possibilities without relying on a single logical estimate. Numerical results show that varying the repetition length provides a tunable trade-off between rate and error-correction performance across a wide range of primary code constructions and their operating regimes. On the decoding side, with the overall LA code held fixed, HLLD reduces the logical error rate by up to 81\%, 75\%, and 69\% for LA codes based on mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively, compared with conventional BP decoding of the same LA codes.

title: WAVES: Wearable Active Vibroacoustic Elasticity Sensing for Low-Cost and Non-Invasive Muscle Stiffness Monitoring
authors: Shubham Rohal (University of California Merced), Dong Yoon Lee (University of California Merced), Shijia Pan (University of California Merced)
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Muscle stiffness is a physiologically meaningful biomarker associated with a wide range of musculoskeletal and neurological conditions. However, existing muscle stiffness assessment methods, such as shear wave elastography (SWE), manual palpation, and handheld mechanical probes, remain impractical for continuous, everyday monitoring due to bulky hardware, operator dependence, and limited self-use. Meanwhile, wearable muscle-sensing modalities such as Electromyography (EMG) and Mechanomyography (MMG) primarily capture muscle activation rather than passive mechanical properties of tissue at rest, leaving a critical gap in portable monitoring of resting muscle stiffness. In this work, we present WAVES, a wearable system for continuous monitoring of muscle stiffness via active vibroacoustic sensing. WAVES injects controlled vibroacoustic excitation into soft tissue and estimates muscle stiffness by measuring shear-wave propagation velocity through Time-Difference-of-Arrival (TDoA) analysis across spatially distributed wearable sensors. To achieve accurate TDoA estimation with low-cost wearable hardware, we develop a physiology- and quality-guided vibroacoustic sensing framework that effectively screens and refines TDoA for accurate stiffness estimation. We evaluate WAVES through characterization experiments using ballistic jelly and end-to-end on-body evaluation with human participants. Results demonstrate that WAVES can robustly estimate muscle stiffness across multiple users and different superficial muscles while enabling lightweight, wearable deployment for everyday use. WAVES is able to achieve a muscle stiffness estimation error of 13.1% or less across multiple users and multiple muscle groups.

title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
authors: Sam Ganzfried
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07089v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.

title: PIT and Reconstruction for Sums of Powers
authors: Nimrod Kaplan, Amir Shpilka, Yann Tal
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study deterministic black-box polynomial identity testing (PIT) and reconstruction for polynomials of the form \[
  f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^r \alpha_i f_i(x)^d, \] where each $f_i$ belongs to some underlying polynomial class $\mathcal{C}$. This representation generalizes Waring decomposition, several natural small-depth circuit models, and polynomial decompositions arising in moment-based learning problems.
  Our main results are three lifting theorems showing that, when the outer power is sufficiently large, PIT and reconstruction for the inner class can be lifted to sums of powers. When the power degree is small, we can perform these tasks directly in some of the cases using closure properties of the underlying models. In particular we obtain the following results:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item When the inner polynomials have bounded-individual-degrees and are sparse, we obtain deterministic reconstruction for every d: the original power-sum decomposition is recovered at high degree, while at low degree the polynomial is reconstructed nonproperly by sparse interpolation.
  \item For sums of powers of same-order and any-order read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs, the same proper/nonproper dichotomy gives deterministic reconstruction for every powering degree.
  \item Explicit quasipolynomial-size hitting sets for every powering degree for several depth-5 and depth-6 circuit families, as well for the models mentioned above.
  Our results for high powering degree rely on the polynomial ABC theorem, which to the best of our knowledge is the first application of this theorem in the context of PIT.

title: Elapsed-Service-Time-Aware Preemption for Age of Information Minimization
authors: Mohammad Moltafet, Nail Akar, Sennur Ulukus, Marian Codreanu, Roy D. Yates
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the age of information and peak age of information in status update systems with an arbitrary number of independent sources sharing a single server with generally distributed service times. We consider a general age-dependent self-preemptive policy in which an in-service update from source $c$ is preempted by a new same-source arrival with a probability $p_c(x)$ that depends on the elapsed service time $x$. This formulation subsumes the non-preemptive, fully self-preemptive, and probabilistically preemptive policies as special cases, and also accommodates threshold-based preemption. We develop a unified analytical framework based on non-homogeneous absorbing continuous-time Markov chains and semi-Markov chains to derive explicit expressions for the average age of information and peak age of information of each source under general per-source service-time distributions and age-dependent preemption rules. The framework applies to both single-source and multi-source systems and enables joint tuning of per-source preemption parameters. Numerical results for fifteen service-time distributions in the single-source setting reveal that the benefits of preemption depend strongly on the service-time hazard-rate structure, with threshold-based preemption providing its most notable additional gains over age-independent policies for distributions with unimodal hazard rates. For a dual-source system with lognormal service times, jointly tuned threshold-based preemption achieves lower sum average age of information and peak age of information than the considered age-independent policies, highlighting the importance of cross-source interactions in preemption decisions.

title: Lossless Source Coding with Marginal Distribution Constraint
authors: Cheuk Ting Li, Jun Chen, Shahab Asoodeh
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider lossless source coding with a marginal distribution constraint on the encoding symbols (SC-MDC). Unlike distribution matching, signal shaping and homophonic coding which require the symbols to be (approximately) i.i.d. following a target distribution, SC-MDC requires each symbol to have a marginal distribution that exactly matches the target distribution, which can be regarded as a perfect perceptual quality constraint on the symbols, and may have applications to wear leveling, source coding with cost and steganography. We give nonasymptotic lower and upper bounds on the optimal encoding length, and exactly characterize the coding rate (or the first-order term of the length) when the source distribution or the target distribution is uniform, or when the source is an i.i.d. sequence.

title: Beyond Proof of Possession: A Relational Theory of Authority
authors: Nicola Gallo
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proof-of-Possession (PoP) establishes that an executor controls an artifact (key, token, credential, or capability), but such control alone determines neither the executor's relational profile nor the causal history of an execution occurrence. We separate PoP from Proof of Relationship (PoR), the semantic property that one execution occurrence validly continues another, and from authorization, which is occurrence-sensitive. The foundational change is in the semantic domain of authorization: from holders and authority-bearing artifacts to execution occurrences situated in causal histories. We give authorization models an observation-based occurrence verdict and a separate transition-admissibility relation; kernel inclusion yields a partial order on observation-kernel classes. Building on Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) and Proof-of-Continuity (PoC), we classify executors by authorization-relevant equivalence relations whose quotients form relational profile spaces, with positive predicates over profile transitions forming a distributive lattice. This adds relational attenuation to authority attenuation: along a valid causal history, $C_{i+1}\subseteq C_i$ and $\rho_{i+1}\Rightarrow\rho_i$. We prove dual monotonicity, combined closure, and origin relational closure. Two occurrences of the same authenticated executor, with the same profile and possession evidence, need not be authorization-equivalent, and within a valid PIC lineage a deputy's independent authority cannot be imported outside the origin context. Finally, we prove that the executor-dependent decision factors through the relational profile and is invariant under sound mechanisms establishing it: successor-side PoP is a possible evidence mechanism, not a necessary premise of authorization. Under explicit Witness Assumptions, a boundary-witnessed checkpoint construction realizes the premises without successor-side PoP.

title: Full Provenance on the COSS Causal Axis: An Event-Level Closure of Causal Attribution and Confused-Deputy Exclusion
authors: Nicola Gallo
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07164v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Provenance Identity Continuity (PIC) represents an authority-use event as an operation/resource behavior situated in a causal lineage, $(o,r,\ell)\in O\times R\times L$. We make the causal occurrence itself primitive: a represented security-relevant causal graph $(E,\to_c)$ in which each occurrence has a unique causal history, so the consistent event-lineage space is canonically isomorphic to $E$. The modeled execution has one causal partial order; distinct lineages are distinct causal histories inside it and may share a root while diverging into incomparable branches. PIC's $O\times R\times L$ is the authority-behavior projection of this space, and Causally Ordered Security-State (COSS) continuity generalizes it to an arbitrary behavior product over the same causal execution. On this semantics we prove an architecture-independent confused-deputy exclusion theorem. PIC continuation requires $C(e')\subseteq C(e)$ on every ordinary causal edge, so descendants are bounded by their ancestors; at an ordinary join, authority available on only one incoming branch cannot be resurrected, even when branches share a common root. Non-conservative combination must be an explicit authorized composition or relaxation event. With protected-effect mediation, an effect caused by request $q$ through an ordinary authority segment can exercise only authority in $C(q)$, so a confused-deputy state is contradictory. The result holds for any system whose protected request-to-effect causes are faithfully represented and whose ordinary authority transport satisfies PIC. We revisit Rajani, Garg, and Rezk: their value, control-flow, and initial-heap attacks are different witnesses of causal ancestry, so full provenance is an evidence mechanism for recovering edges of the causal graph, not the foundation of the PIC theorem. Finally we lift it to the COSS product of heterogeneous security-state coordinates.

title: Global Surveillance Under the Lens: Reconstructing Passive Dolev-Yao Intruders
authors: Paolo Modesti
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Global surveillance systems record large volumes of network traffic for retrospective analysis, but packet captures alone reveal little about protocol-level semantics. This paper presents an automated, specification-guided methodology for reconstructing passive Dolev-Yao intruder executions from captured network traffic and validating the reconstructed executions against a formal protocol specification. The framework takes a PCAP capture, an AnBx specification, and the associated deployment metadata; it extracts Java-serialised objects from TCP streams, reconstructs protocol sessions and channel-to-step assignments, and generates a passive intruder that evaluates the Dolev-Yao derived checks produced by the AnBx compiler. Three reconstruction challenges are addressed: multiple serialised objects and object references within a TCP stream, ambiguity in mapping interleaved connections to concurrent protocol sessions, and semantic validation of candidate reconstructions. We evaluate the methodology on 121 protocols from the AnBx test suite. For single-session captures, the standard JDK cryptographic provider recovers 97.8% of expected objects and achieves 94.2% successful reconstruction, where success requires complete object recovery and a clean passive-intruder execution. For the 112 parallel-capable protocols, the toolchain achieves 89.3% successful reconstruction for both two and three concurrent sessions, while recovering approximately 97.2% of expected objects. Experiments with mismatched protocol-role mappings and deliberately mutated traces show that the generated Dolev-Yao checks respond to semantic inconsistencies. By making the reconstruction step explicit, the solution produces protocol-level observations on which assessments of protocol resilience and the design of defensive countermeasures can be built.

title: A Complete Equational Theory for Quantum Circuits with Generalized Control
authors: William Schober (Universit\`a della Svizzera italiana), Scott Wesley (Dalhousie University)
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controlled subcircuits are commonplace in quantum algorithms as they represent the quantum analogue of branching statements (if then). We introduce a generalization of controlled subcircuits in the form of a binary operation which sends pairs of unitary quantum circuits to a generalized controlled operation, whose semantics are based on matrix exponentials and logarithms. The family of quantum circuits with generalized controlled operations and circuit exponentiation is denoted HQC for Hierarchical Quantum Circuits. We formalize HQC as a modified prop category using a novel category-theoretic construction, and provide a sound and complete equational theory for diagrammatic reasoning in HQC.

title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
authors: Woosang Lim (SAINT Machines, KAIST), Yeseul Chang (Chung-Ang University), Jaewoo Lee (Chung-Ang University)
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

title: Quadratic Extractors
authors: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jesse Goodman, David Zuckerman
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A quadratic source is a random variable $X\sim\mathbb{F}_2^n$ generated by applying $n$ quadratics to a hidden uniform string. Previously, the best-known explicit extractor for this model required min-entropy roughly $k=n-\sqrt{\log n}$. In this paper, we give an explicit construction for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. Even for the special case of $2$-local sources, where each bit of $X$ depends on two hidden uniform bits, achieving an entropy requirement below $k=\sqrt{n}$ was an important open problem. This is because such sources provably cannot be reduced (in a black-box manner) to our most powerful general-purpose seedless extractor, known as a sumset extractor. Our new extractor bypasses this barrier, providing the first explicit construction to go beyond sumset extraction.

title: Degree profiles of uniform polynomial consequences: Linear lower bounds for Nullstellensatz and Polynomial Calculus
authors: S{\o}ren Riis
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07280v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper proves asymptotically optimal linear degree lower bounds for Nullstellensatz and Polynomial Calculus, yielding a four-way polynomial-versus-exponential proof-size classification for uniform polynomial consequences over fields of positive characteristic. The size bounds use full, explicit coefficient lists, including zeros.
  Apart from a fixed finite initial range, exactly one of four cases occurs: $\mathrm T_1$, bounded degree; $\mathrm T_2$, degree at least linear in the universe size $n$; $\mathrm T_3$, constant degree on some residue classes and at least linear degree on the others; or $\mathrm T_4$, infinitely many recurring finite degrees, with bounded-degree subsequences and finite $\Omega(n)$ peaks at arbitrarily large sizes. Thus the size patterns are polynomial bounds, exponential lower bounds, a periodic mixture, or polynomial subsequences with finite exponential peaks, respectively. Underivable targets have degree $\infty$, and both proof systems assign the same type.
  The result strengthens my 2008--2009 refutation classification and extends it to uniform consequences. The proof uses degree-preserving lifting with onset and period bounds linear in the degree. A common $p$-adic hardness spectrum describes the four types topologically. Distinguishing any two types is undecidable already for refutations. The linear degree bounds, four-way classification and pairwise undecidability results have been formalised and verified in Lean. The Lean formalisation, verification records and an accompanying tutorial are available in the supporting materials (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23965838).

title: A New Characterization of Streaming Decidability of Boolean CSPs Under Deletions
authors: Aditya Bandekar, Amatya Sharma, Santhoshini Velusamy
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We characterize the single-pass streaming space complexity of Boolean CSP satisfiability in the strict-turnstile model for every fixed constraint language $\Gamma$ of $k$-ary Boolean relations that is not trivially satisfiable. Constraints can be inserted or deleted with nonnegative multiplicities; satisfiability is decided for those remaining at the end.
  While Sharma and Velusamy [ESA 2026] characterized insertion-only complexity via non-redundancy (up to logarithmic factors), we show that strict-turnstile complexity is governed by the integer capturing degree. For $R\subseteq\{0,1\}^k$, let $d_R$ be the minimum degree of an integer-coefficient polynomial vanishing exactly on $R$ over the Boolean hypercube, and set $d_\Gamma=\max_{R\in\Gamma}d_R$. On polynomial-length streams, we obtain an $O_k(n^{d_\Gamma}\operatorname{polylog} n)$-space randomized algorithm and an $\Omega_k(n^{d_\Gamma}/\log n)$ lower bound for all algorithms. Moreover, our algorithm outputs a sparse instance preserving every satisfying assignment.
  This yields, to our knowledge, the first insertion-only versus turnstile separation for streaming CSPs. It also differs from the Fourier-degree characterization of exact optimization by Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu [ITCS 2023]. For $k\ge3$, $k$-XOR with literals has three distinct space complexities: $\widetilde\Theta(n)$ for insertion-only satisfiability, $\widetilde\Theta(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})$ for strict-turnstile satisfiability, and $\widetilde\Theta(n^k)$ for exact optimization in either model.

title: Asymptotic advantage of quantum one-way and SMP communication for total functions
authors: Dmytro Gavinsky
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We exhibit a total Boolean function on n input bits whose bounded-error quantum simultaneous-message (and hence one-way) communication complexity is in O(\sqrt n), whereas its randomised one-way (and hence simultaneous-message) communication complexity is in \Omega(n). The same function admits a classical simultaneous-message protocol of cost O(\sqrt n) when the players share O(\sqrt n) EPR pairs.

title: Functional Converses for Private Matrix-Product Retrieval under Library-Wide Decoder-Side Correlation
authors: Malihe Aliasgari, Yousef Nejatbakhsh
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07325v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider private retrieval of the matrix product $A^\top B^{(\theta)}$ from replicated $P_c$-colluding servers when $B^{(\ell)}=A+N^{(\ell)}$, with the innovations mutually independent and independent of the user-held $A\in\mathbb{F}_q^{m\times m}$. The servers store the full library, correlated with $A$, which changes both the communication problem and the security definition: a secrecy condition including the stored library cannot hold, as the library itself partly reveals $A$. We therefore measure only additional leakage and require index privacy conditioned on $A$; both reduce to classical notions under independence. For $A$ of rank $k<m$ we prove, with no structural hypothesis on the map, $D^*\geq H(A^\top B^{(\theta)}\mid A)/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}(N,P_c,L)-o(km)$, where $C_{\mathrm{PIR}}(N,P_c,L)$ is the replicated $P_c$-colluding private-information-retrieval capacity. The proof rests on a colluding converse for servers storing arbitrary refinements of the demanded messages, whose answers need not be measurable functions of the functional-message library, and a privacy-transfer characterization. Publishing a canonical row-space representative makes the bound achievable for arbitrary independent and identically distributed innovations under a public-setup measure. Under a strengthened observational model (exact correctness, common conditional library support, and full-transcript security), concealment forces $D\geq H(G_m N^{(\theta)})/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}$, where $G_m$ spans the linear join of all row spaces in the support of the operand distribution; this extends to vanishing error under a simultaneous-decodability assumption. In the full-rank case product recovery reduces to innovation recovery: $D^*=H(N^{(\theta)})/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}+o(m^2)$.

title: Energy-Time Optimal Decoding Using Expander-Graph LDPC Codes and Mesh Network Architecture
authors: Christopher Blake
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07336v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Within the Thompson VLSI model, the first energy optimal decoding schemes (up to polylogarithmic factors) that also reach clock cycle lower bounds are constructed. Let $N$ be block length. Then, there is an exponential error scaling function and a binary symmetric channel, such that for all $f(N)$ that scales to zero more slowly than this, there is a decoding scheme for this channel with error probability that scales as $O(f(N))$ that has number of clock cycles $T\le O(\sqrt{-\log(f(N)})\text{polylog}(N))$ and energy $E\le O(N\sqrt{-\log(f(N))}\text{polylog}(N))$. This matches fundamental lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The technique uses expander-graph based LDPC codes, a mesh network architecture, and a parallelization technique. The key technical result needed for this is a lemma in graph theory. This lemma is used to show that communication graphs of bounded node degree can be routed through two- and three-dimensional mesh networks without overflowing the memory of any mesh node. Upper bounds are also extended to three dimensions.

title: Breaking $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ via Adaptive Neuron Clustering in Cryptanalytic Model Extraction
authors: Haojie Wu, Haolin Liu, Tianshuo Cong, Guoyan Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cryptanalytic model extraction poses a fundamental threat to deep learning model confidentiality by enabling precise parameter recovery with theoretical guarantees of functional equivalence. To counter this growing threat, $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$ (NeurIPS 2025) was proposed as the first dedicated defense against cryptanalytic extraction and remains the only defense believed to be effective to date. It encourages neurons to learn similar weights so that they switch activation states together, making their individual contributions harder to distinguish. However, we notice that neurons with similar weights need not switch activation states together under small perturbations. Instead, weight similarity can cause the original clustering rule to merge signatures from distinct neurons when only a subset of their normalized weight coordinates agree. Motivated by this observation, we introduce $\mathsf{SimBreak}$, an adaptive clustering rule that breaks the weight-similarity defense of $\mathsf{TraintoDefend}$. $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ estimates a relative scale from all jointly observed weight coordinates and uses the same scale to test both weight direction and bias consistency. Across six protected fully connected networks trained on MNIST, $\mathsf{SimBreak}$ raises target layer signature recovery from $0\%$ to $100\%$, with a maximum relative recovery error of $2^{-22.27}$. Our work challenges the use of neuron weight similarity as a sufficient basis for protection and establishes adaptive evaluation as essential to assessing cryptanalytic extraction defenses.

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
authors: Hans-Martin Will
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement.
  The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families, and an intensional identity type. Proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule, so proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system---confluent, injective on type formers, and decidable by a type-free test---while a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant function types, and declared class inclusions.
  We prove consistency via a set-theoretic model; develop a justification logic over the kernel's propositions to track evidence and support; organize environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms and external verdicts enter via comorphisms; formulate a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes, and refinements; and prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation, and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. A Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.

title: Information-Spectrum General Formulas for the Capacity Region of Classical-Quantum Multiple Access Channels
authors: Takuya Kubo, Hiroshi Nagaoka
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07462v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For classical-quantum multiple access channels (cq-MACs) with two senders, we give several general expressions for the capacity region, valid for arbitrary sequences of channels. In the case of asymptotically vanishing error ($\varepsilon=0$), the capacity region is expressed in terms of spectral inf-mutual information rates. For every $0\le\varepsilon<1$, the $\varepsilon$-capacity region is expressed in terms of a quantity defined through a linear combination of three alternative hypotheses. In particular, the outer bound of Kubo and Nagaoka (2015) is tight. Our results include the quantum counterpart of the general formula of Han (1998) for the classical MAC. The most important ingredient is the one-shot inner bound of Sen (2021), which we apply to each member of an arbitrary channel sequence.

title: Polynomial-Time Approximate EFX for Chores via Flow and Matching
authors: Genjie Qin, Qizhi Fang, Minming Li, Wenjing Liu, Xin Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07468v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a complete $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation for any rational $0<\varepsilon\leq1$, improving the previous approximation guarantee from a factor depending on the number of agents to a constant. The algorithm extends to EF$k$X, achieving a $(2+1/k+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every integer $k\geq1$.
  For instances with relatively few chores, the polynomial-time BRBI algorithm gives stronger guarantees. It finds exact EF$k$X allocations when $m\leq2kn$ and achieves a factor of at most $2-1/k$ when $m\le(3k-1)n$. In particular, $k=1$ and $m\leq2n$ give exact EFX.
  We further show that the approximation factor \(2+1/k\) is asymptotically tight for our main algorithm. We also construct a four-agent, ten-chore instance in which every complete allocation has EFX approximation factor at least $11/10$, improving upon the $20/19$ lower bound for submodular costs even under additive costs.

title: AMORT-V1: Checkpointed Post-Quantum Attestation for Industrial Controllers
authors: Rishabh Das, Gerald Agendia, Jibriel Adjei, Ahmed Oun
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07476v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Programmable logic controllers often remain deployed for decades, making post-quantum attestation a long-term requirement. Prior measurements of OpenPLC attestation show that post-quantum signing can consume 88--99% of round-trip latency and that durable state can further limit throughput. We introduce AMORT-V1, a checkpointed attestation protocol that moves public-key signing and durable commitment from individual reports to periodic checkpoints. An ML-KEM epoch establishes per-device evidence keys, devices authenticate reports with MACs, and the controller commits ordered evidence through hash-chained Merkle checkpoints signed with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA. Because shared MACs do not provide transferable proof of device origin, AMORT-V1 adds a device-held disclosure chain whose keys are released after checkpoint commitment. We validate the protocol with a 27-case attack matrix, 149 differential-test vectors, and a seven-node Raspberry Pi 5 testbed with five physical OpenPLC provers. Checkpointing reduces controller cost by 90 times relative to per-report ML-DSA without durable logging and by 878 times when durable logging is required. Transferable device-origin verification costs 2.95micro sec per report, while controller-side scaling to 10,000 identities requires 6.18 micro sec and 155 octets per report. AMORT-V1 also supports rollback-resistant restart through TPM-backed monotonic state without placing durable hardware operations on the per-report path.

title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
authors: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07483v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.

title: MEvince: Knowledge-Constrained LLM Reasoning for Technique Identification from Malware Reports
authors: Hongyu She, Yiling He, Mengda Xie, Yiping Liu, Xingzhi Qian, Zhan Qin, Lorenzo Cavallaro
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07486v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mapping behavioral intelligence in malware analysis reports to ATT&CK techniques supports threat analysis and defense, but reliable identification remains challenging. Supporting evidence is often scattered across long, heterogeneous reports, while closely related techniques share behavioral cues and differ only in subtle but decisive details. While large language models (LLMs) can use external knowledge to interpret reports, they may assign techniques based on plausible associations rather than sufficient evidence. We present MEvince, a knowledge-constrained LLM reasoning framework for report-level malware technique identification. Its core is a shared behavioral representation connecting report observations to technique definitions. This representation is built through agentic mining of technique documentation and supports two online stages: 1) primitive-guided extraction uses behavioral primitives to structure LLM-extracted observations, link them to source passages, and group dispersed evidence; 2) evidence-aligned retrieval matches this evidence to technique profiles through the same concepts, retaining likely candidates and confusable alternatives for LLM comparison of distinguishing behaviors. Controls at both stages validate evidence references and check technique-specific requirements. The representation also supports adaptation without parameter updates, where offline agentic audits diagnose concept weaknesses and refine extraction or retrieval policies. We evaluate MEvince against 11 baselines spanning four method families using a dataset of 610 public malware reports referenced by MITRE ATT&CK. MEvince improves exact-ID F1 over the strongest baseline by 17.4%, and its concept-guided retrieval increases gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%. With a small adaptation set, offline refinement yields further gains and outperforms baselines that update model parameters.

title: Transparency in Team Contracts
authors: Paul D\"utting, Yingkai Li, Inbal Talgam-Cohen, Jinzhao Wu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07494v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools.
  We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular.
  The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of $2.311$, and thus a $3.081$-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.

title: JailBound: FOL-Guided Jailbreak Evaluation for Exploring LLM Behavioral Boundaries
authors: Fazong Wu, Xin Wang, Ming Yang, Zhenyong Zhang, Xiaoming Wu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07530v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as general-purpose conversational assistants, they must handle diverse user requests while reliably refusing harmful ones. Jailbreak attacks craft adversarial instructions or conversational contexts to elicit unsafe responses despite these safeguards. However, existing jailbreak benchmarks often rely on manually designed or collected prompts, making it difficult to systematically extend coverage to new threat conditions. Moreover, existing attack search methods typically optimize for attack success rate (ASR), providing limited insight into how model behavior changes locally between safe refusal and unsafe response. To address these limitations, we present JailBound, a unified jailbreak evaluation framework that combines automated benchmark construction with first-order loss (FOL)-guided dual-branch search. JailBound organizes threats by risk category, application domain, and attack type. Conditioned on this taxonomy, a fine-tuned meta-attack generator synthesizes evaluation prompts across diverse threat conditions. FOL serves as a local sensitivity signal for exploring high-value attack states and behavior-sensitive states. We evaluate JailBound across 46 LLMs from 13 model families under a unified experimental protocol. Under matched settings, the High-Value Branch improves average ASR over a ZOL-only baseline by 5.1 and 4.9 percentage points across the two evaluation settings. Under local perturbations, states from the Safety-Sensitivity Branch exhibit higher behavioral flip rates than those from the High-Value Branch across all tested radii for JailBound and S-Eval, indicating greater local sensitivity of judge-assigned safety labels. Warning: this paper includes examples that may be offensive or harmful.

title: Cores of $3$-distant convex games
authors: Keisuke Bando, Toshiyuki Hirai, Kenzo Imamura, Ryuhei Mizutani
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.

title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
authors: Asr{\i}n Efe Yorulmaz, Tamer Ba\c{s}ar
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07589v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

title: Combinatorial limitations of list-decoding Reed-Solomon codes
authors: Omar Alrabiah, Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07607v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: For infinitely many rates $R \in (0,1)$, we show that full-length Reed-Solomon codes over fields of low characteristic can contain super-polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of radius just exceeding the Johnson radius. Over prime fields, we exhibit full-length Reed-Solomon codes of constant rate $R$ with polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of relative radius bounded strictly below $1-R$. This refutes a recent conjecture that, over prime fields, list sizes below capacity are always bounded by a constant. Together, these results demonstrate that certain restrictions in recent works on explicit Reed-Solomon codes achieving list-decoding capacity, related to the choice of field or evaluation points or to the list-size guarantee, are inherent.

title: A Gingerbread House for LLM Agents: Source-Planned Honeypots That Lure Autonomous Attackers into an Isolated Shadow
authors: Seungdeok Roh, Seokjun Ryu, Sohee Park, Daeseon Choi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents can exploit web vulnerabilities fast enough that patching may come too late. Deception against such agents has mostly lured them away from a real target that stays reachable. We study a different arrangement: an LLM defender plans a static honeypot from the application's source, and a router sends every later request of a client it confirms as an attacker, including a working exploit, to an isolated shadow copy. We compare no defence, this static plan, and an augmented configuration with a runtime LLM responder and further router rules, graded by the benchmark's own grader on the real target and, for ARTEX, also on the shadow. On the 40 critical CVE-Bench tasks the static plan cut real compromise from 26/40 to 5/40 for Claude Opus 4.8 and from 20/40 to 0/40 (31 valid runs) for the ARTEX attack framework. On 20 new tasks not used in the design, ARTEX went from 15/20 to 0/20. In about half of the deception-arm runs ARTEX's exploit succeeded on the shadow while the real target stayed intact: the defence moved a working exploit rather than stopping it, and the remaining risk lies in requests that reach the real target before confirmation. ARTEX reported a planted fake secret as genuine on 30 of the 120 deception-arm tasks, five times in a report that labelled another item a decoy. With ARTEX's real compromise at zero in both deception configurations, they did not differ significantly on the remaining outcomes, a comparison that does not isolate the responder.

title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
authors: Rongting Zhang, Martin Bertran, Sandeep Avula, Chia-Jung Lee, Vanessa Murdock
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at https://github.com/amazon-science/task-tampering-prompt-injection.

title: A Universal Threshold Theory for Local Properties of Random Linear Codes
authors: Vinayak M. Kumar, Ray Li, Jonathan Mosheiff, Gilad Shavit
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Thresholds for local properties tell us which guarantees to expect from random linear codes (RLCs) and help us carry those guarantees over to structured codes. A monotone property is $b$-local if a collection of at most $b$ codewords can witness its satisfaction or failure, as in list decoding and list recovery. The threshold of $\mathcal P$ is the code dimension at which the probability that an RLC in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ satisfies $\mathcal P$ crosses $1/2$ in a sharp transition. We show that the threshold of a $b$-local property $\mathcal P$ is within $O(b)$ dimensions of the expectation threshold. This is the dimension predicted by the best union bound over covers of $\mathcal P$: families of subspaces such that the span of every witness contains at least one member.
  This gives a general derandomization statement: Any decreasing local property satisfied by RLCs at a given rate holds at a similar rate for pseudorandom ensembles that fool the cover union bound. In addition to previously studied ensembles, these include codes whose parity-check matrix is sampled from a small-bias distribution. Because our threshold characterization applies to all local properties, this derandomization also reaches properties beyond the scope of earlier reductions, including maximum loads in linear hashing for arbitrary input sets, rank-metric list decoding, and list decoding from insertion-deletion errors and burst errors.
  Our theorem unifies and strengthens prior works on row-symmetric and coordinate-wise linear characterizations, which located the threshold to within $O(q^{2b}\log_q n)$ and $O(b^2+nb/\log_2 q)$ dimensions, respectively. We obtain $O(b)$ error for every $b$-local property, independently of alphabet size. Under suitable pseudorandomness bounds, the rate loss vanishes for every $b=o(n)$, compared to $b=O(\log n)$ for earlier frameworks.

title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
authors: Liang Ran, Huaqing Li, Lifeng Zheng, Jun Li, Run Tang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07703v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate $o(1/k)$ in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.

title: Over-the-Scene Computation: Illumination-Programmed Functional Sensing of Unresolvable Populations
authors: Seyed Mohammad Azimi-Abarghouyi, Christopher G. Brinton
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07732v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decisions about dense populations depend on how much will cross a boundary by a deadline and when the first member arrives. Conventional radar forms a range-Doppler map, whose cells add noise and whose detections merge unresolved members. We introduce over-the-scene computation, where illumination makes the scene compute such functionals without resolving members. With random echo phases, a correlator's mean output energy sums member reflectivities weighted by a kernel set by the waveform and template. The waveform's ambiguity function is this computation's transfer function, determining computable functionals and their noise cost. One readout aggregates members over a small delay-Doppler area but along a line segment growing with duration, longest for the chirp of matching slope among constant-envelope waveforms. Members predicted to share a range lie on such a line, so a chirp's mean beat spectrum is the predicted range profile at a look-ahead horizon set by its rate. For unbiased estimation, a Cramer-Rao bound over all equal-energy waveforms favors resolving members above unit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and grouping weaker ones into unit-SNR sets. At 0.65 members per cell, -10 dB member SNR, and one sweep, the chirp's bin sum inside the boundary comes within 16% of this bound in root-mean-square error and, with 77 times fewer samples per horizon, outperforms every unbiased estimator from a coherent processing interval of equal dwell, bandwidth, and energy. No finite set of waveform-template probes determines an unconstrained Rayleigh-fluctuating population's first arrival, but bisection localizes it if first arrivals outweigh later arrivals' sidelobes.

title: Multiplicative and Additive Extractors for Low Entropy Samplable Sources Under Reduced Assumptions
authors: Marshall Ball, Eshan Chattopadhyay, Mohit Gurumukhani, Ronen Shaltiel, Yunya Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07829v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Trevisan and Vadhan [TV, FOCS'00] constructed (seedless) extractors for distributions samplable by poly-size circuits that have very high min-entropy, under the very strong complexity theoretic hardness assumption that $\mathsf{E}=\mathsf{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})$ requires size $2^{\Omega(n)}$ circuits that have oracle access to $\Sigma_6^{\text{P}}$. In this paper we give three new explicit constructions of extractors for samplable distributions.
  First, we construct an extractor that extracts one bit, with constant error, for min-entropy $k=O(\log n)$, which matches the non-constructive probabilistic argument. This result uses hardness for nondeterministic circuits, and achieves the same parameters as the recent extractor of Oh and Shaltiel [OS, STOC'26] under an incomparable hardness assumption. In contrast to the extractor of [OS26], our extractor (and, similarly, the constructions below) also works for the more general class of distributions samplable with postselection (a model introduced by [BGDM, FOCS'23] that generalizes samplable and recognizable sources).
  Second, we construct an extractor that extracts almost all the entropy, with polynomially small error, for min-entropy $k=n^{\alpha}$, where $\alpha>0$ is an arbitrary constant. This result also uses hardness for nondeterministic circuits, and significantly improves upon the recent extractor of [Shaltiel, FOCS'25] which required a much stronger assumption. This extractor is also \textit{multiplicative}: a stronger notion suggested in [AASY, Comp. Complexity'16; Shaltiel, CCC'25] to make extractors for samplable distributions suitable for selecting keys for cryptographic protocols.
  Third, we construct an extractor that extracts almost all the entropy, with polynomially small error, for min-entropy $k=\mathrm{polylog}(n)$. This result uses hardness for circuits that have oracle access to $\Sigma_2^{\text{P}}$.

title: CANMentor: A Large-Small Model Collaboration Framework for CAN Bus Intrusion Detection
authors: Zhiquan Liu (the College of Cyber Security, Jinan University), Haolin Gao (the College of Cyber Security, Jinan University), Bo Wu (the College of Cyber Security, Jinan University), Jingjing Guo (the School of Cyber Engineering, Xidian University), Heng Sun (the College of Information Science and Technology, Jinan University), Jianfeng Ma (the School of Cyber Engineering, Xidian University)
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07853v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Controller Area Network (CAN) bus lacks built-in security mechanisms, making real-time intrusion detection necessary. However, resource and latency constraints limit vehicle-side intrusion detection systems (IDSs) to lightweight models, whose detection performance and generalization can degrade under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. Meanwhile, uploading original CAN messages to the cloud for more powerful model inference risks exposing sensitive vehicle information. We propose CANMentor, a large-small model collaboration framework in which a cloud-side large language model (LLM) teacher supervises vehicle-side lightweight IDS models for CAN bus intrusion detection. Each vehicle first performs local inference, and a privacy-aware generator then produces proxies from the original CAN messages for cloud-side teacher inference to protect data privacy. The vehicle uses the teacher prediction only when the response arrives within a prescribed latency bound and otherwise retains the local prediction; all returned teacher logits are converted into soft targets for periodic knowledge distillation. On non-IID partitions of the ROAD dataset and the HCRL Car-Hacking dataset, knowledge distillation yields maximum relative Macro F1 improvements of 25.01% and 20.79%, respectively. Teacher predictions also improve detection accuracy for CAN messages near the local decision boundary by 38.71-42.00 percentage points.

title: Quantum Communication and Phase Sensing over a Dephasing Channel with Thermal Noise
authors: Nikos A. Mitsiou, Ioannis Krikidis
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dephasing is a prominent source of decoherence in quantum communication, degrading phase coherence and transmission reliability. Therefore, knowledge of the physical channel parameters for reliable transmission is imperative, motivating the integration of quantum communication and sensing at the physical layer. Consequently, we study the transmission of coherent states over a von Mises dephasing channel affected by thermal noise. We consider a heterodyne receiver, for which, we first derive the symbol-error probability (SEP) and an accurate closed-form approximation, through which an irreducible asymptotic error floor due to the dephasing channel is identified. We note that the derived SEP is affected by the mismatch between the receiver's mean phase estimation and the true mean phase, thereby formalizing the interplay between sensing accuracy and communication reliability. In addition, we derive the Fisher information (FI) for the mean phase acquisition of the channel and provide closed-form lower and upper FI bounds. Moreover, the quantum FI (QFI) of the channel is studied, and lower and upper bounds on the QFI are given, which become asymptotically tight as the photon number increases. Despite the initial complexity of the FI and the QFI, the bounds given are relatively simple and effective. In addition, by comparing the FI with the QFI, we show that heterodyne detection approaches the quantum sensing limit as the number of photons increase, while an unavoidable sensing floor exists due to dephasing. Then, using the SEP and the FI analysis, we discuss the conditions under which communication and phase estimation requirements are jointly feasible. Finally, numerical results validate the derived SEP, estimation bounds, and the sensing-communication feasibility tradeoff.

title: Operational Indirect Rate-Distortion Functions for Classification Tasks
authors: Yann Miguet, Elsa Dupraz, Philippe Mary
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In goal-oriented communications, indirect source coding involves two sources: a semantic source $X$ and an observation $Z$, which is the only source available at the encoder. In this paper, we consider this framework for classification, where the decoder only needs to reconstruct $X$. We argue that the gap between the indirect rate-distortion function and the performance of practical learned coding schemes, such as variational information bottleneck (VIB) and variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures, comes from three effects: the latent representation, the choice of the deep neural network (DNN) architecture and training loss, and whether the encoder is aware of the task. To quantify these effects, we introduce four operational rate-distortion functions that account for the DNN architecture and the training loss, and we establish a hierarchy among them. We then derive these functions for a Gaussian mixture source, where $X$ is the mixture state. Numerical results, both for the Gaussian mixture and for practical coding schemes on the CIFAR-100 dataset, quantify the rate loss incurred by each effect.

title: A Little Derandomization Goes a Long Way: Unconditional Circuit Lower Bounds using Low-Degree PIT
authors: Nikolai Chukhin, Karthik Gajulapalli, Alexander Golovnev, Ivan Mihajlin

title: Stealthy Malicious Interference Detection in UAV Formations: A Power-Domain Signaling Game Approach
authors: Jianle Ba, Shaolong Guo, Yuntao Wang, Xin Wu, Zhou Su, Zhendong Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.07977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable intra-swarm communication is fundamental to cooperative sensing, control, and mission execution in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms. In open low-altitude shared-spectrum environments, coexisting UAVs may cause benign interference through spectrum reuse and signal leakage, while jamming UAVs may deliberately degrade critical intra-swarm links. Since a jamming UAV can adjust its transmit power to disguise signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) degradation as link fluctuation in benign interference, stealthy jammer UAV detection remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a novel belief-driven stealthy jammer UAV detection scheme from the perspective of Bayesian security game. To capture stealthy interference in shared-spectrum UAV swarms, the interfering UAV is modeled as a hidden benign or jamming type, whose transmit power strategy induces the SINR observed by the defender. The defender updates its posterior belief from the observed SINR and decides whether to maintain normal operation or trigger defensive power boosting. We characterize pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibrium (PBE) conditions under separating structures with distinguishable type and pooling structures with indistinguishable observations. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme improves the defender's expected utility compared to the conventional schemes.

title: KeHoSu: Keyed Homoglyph Substitution for Authenticated Text Provenance over Copy-Paste Channels
authors: Andrei Alexandru Dr\u{a}ghici, Sediola Ruko, Briland Hitaj, Dorjan Hitaj
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Nowadays, large language models produce text at scale, and much of it is redistributed across platforms. A moderator who finds a suspicious comment, post or article may want to know which platform generated it and for which account. In this paper we study attribution over the channel through which such text actually travels, copy-paste, which discards document metadata but keeps Unicode code points. We present KeHoSu, which turns the confusable characters of homoglyph attacks into a keyed attribution channel: the variant chosen for each carrier letter encodes one bit of an identifier made of a platform field, a user field and a truncated authentication tag. Moreover, given that reshared text is often quoted in fragments, and the placement therefore keeps no positional state, we show that KeHoSu is invariant to sentence reordering up to a constant boundary layer and depends on a partial quotation only through the retained length. We characterize the code-point channel by its capacity, removability and detectability, and provide an achievable region that relates the three. We evaluate KeHoSu over a wide range of use cases and show that the mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms, attributing the majority of all excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters (about two sentences) on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters (about one sentence) on standard English prose.

title: Cloudy Skies: Early Detection of Jamming Against Iridium LEO Satellite-IoT Links
authors: Ingrid Huso, Giulia Fliescher, Savio Sciancalepore, Gabriele Oligeri
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08118v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite-IoT systems increasingly provide connectivity to mobile assets in remote areas, which makes their resilience to radio-frequency jamming a growing concern. Timely jamming detection, i.e., before complete link failure, has been studied for terrestrial networks and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), but it remains unclear whether these approaches are effective on LEO links, where propagation varies rapidly, the received signal is weak, and jamming should be detected from the messages that are still correctly received. This paper investigates the extent to which jamming of Iridium LEO satellite-IoT links can be detected from the physical layer of correctly decoded messages. To this aim, we collect and publicly release a real-world dataset of Iridium messages under 47 jamming conditions, spanning two propagation environments, static and mobile receivers, and different jammer distances, powers, and signal types. We use this dataset to analyze three one-class autoencoder-based anomaly detectors operating on physical-layer information and compare them against two signal-quality estimators commonly used as jamming indicators in GNSS-based applications. Our results show that detectability is governed by the rise of the receiver noise floor, through which jammer power, distance, and receiver mobility act. With 1000-sample chunks, i.e., 40 ms of received signal at 25,000 samples per second (about four correctly decoded messages), the autoencoders reach an AUC of at least 0.84 whenever a noise jammer raises the noise floor by at least 9 dB, whereas the $C/N_0$ and SNR estimators fail, since received messages, although correctly decoded, retain a high SNR under jamming. Therefore, timely jamming detection for LEO satellite-IoT links like Iridium should rely on physical-layer information beyond the signal-quality metrics adopted in the GNSS domain.

title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition
authors: Niels Van Santen, Yves Rosseel, Daniele Marinazzo
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources' information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.

title: Drift-Resilient Predictive Interference Management: Online Adaptation of an Extreme-Value Predictor
authors: Aamir Mahmood, Fateme Salehi, Nurul Huda Mahmood, Song Han
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Predictive interference management supports ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) by allocating finite-blocklength resources against a high conditional quantile of next-slot interference. Building on an extreme-value-theory/kernel-density-estimation (EVT/KDE) predictor with quantile-defined interference states, this paper makes the predictor resilient to unannounced shifts in the interference distribution. Its cumulative refitting on all past observations does not specify how the state partition and retained samples should evolve after a regime change. We show that drift first makes the quantile partition inefficient: cumulative refitting preserves tail support and coverage but cannot recover conditional resolution, and pays for it in channel use, whereas discarding history starves the tail estimator. We therefore propose event-triggered quantile-space adaptation. A nonparametric cumulative sum (CUSUM) on the predictor's level stream detects change. At each confirmed event, the quantile partition is re-derived from post-change observations, retained history is re-binned under it, and each state is refit from a bounded per-state memory, capped to balance stale-regime bias against tail-estimation variance, with a closed-form L-moment tail estimator. At a nominal coverage target $\eta\!=\!0.99$, relative to matched cumulative refitting with fixed states, the proposed method reduces channel use by $5.7$--$13.2\%$ and quantile pinball loss by $25$--$50\%$ across abrupt, incremental, compound, downward, and reversal drift, with coverage changing by $-0.5$ to $+1.0$ percentage points. At matched achieved coverage, it saves $4$--$18\%$ of channel uses, while resource use in load-only and stationary cases changes by less than $0.5\%$. With $K$ samples per state and $L$ states, predictor memory is bounded at $O(KL)$ rather than growing as $O(t)$.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Dependent Graph Classes
authors: Jan Dreier, Nikolas M\"ahlmann, Szymon Toru\'nczyk
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08143v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monadically dependent graph classes are those in which first-order logic cannot encode all graphs. They include all nowhere dense classes and all classes of bounded twin-width. We show that first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on every monadically dependent graph class. Together with the known hardness result for hereditary classes that are not monadically dependent, this gives a complete characterization of the hereditary graph classes with fixed-parameter tractable first-order model checking. This resolves a central open problem in algorithmic model theory. Our proof combines ideas from structural graph theory (graph decompositions), finite model theory (locality of first-order logic), and model theory (counting types). In particular, we show that in monadically dependent classes, tuples of fixed length have only $|U|^{O(1)}$ types of fixed quantifier rank over any set of parameters $U$.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
authors: Yalin E. Sagduyu, Tugba Erpek, Aylin Yener
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: The Promise of Strategic Agentic Scambaiting
authors: Abhishek Satyam, Hossein Siadati, Haadi Jafarian, Sima Jafarikhah, Juntao Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08170v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scammers have increasingly adopted AI-driven capabilities, evolving from automated message generation to fully agentic conversational systems that scale operations and maximize the exploitation of fraudulent resources before detection and takedown. In parallel, agentic scambaiting has emerged as a defensive approach in which autonomous agents impersonate potential victims and engage scammers in sustained interactions to extract actionable threat intelligence, such as mule bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallet addresses, that can be reported to disrupt fraudulent infrastructures. Together, these developments transform online fraud into an adversarial socio-technical ecosystem in which autonomous scamming and scambaiting agents engage in deceptive interactions while competing over the discovery, preservation, and exploitation of one another's resources. A fundamental and largely unexplored question is how defensive scambaiting can remain effective in an agent-to-agent environment, and under what conditions either side gains a strategic advantage. In this paper, we present a formal model of agent-to-agent fraud interactions that captures the strategic decision spaces available to both attackers and defenders. Using this framework, we analyze the dynamics of engagement, resource consumption, belief adaptation, and disruption outcomes. We find that scammer profitability turns negative once baiting-agent prevalence exceeds certain thresholds, and that when both sides improve at the same pace, defender investment in mimicry quality outpaces equivalent gains in scammer detection capability, so the arms race favors the defender under our baseline parameters. Our model and findings provide insights into the stability, scalability, and long-term effectiveness of autonomous defensive agents in an evolving AI-mediated fraud landscape.

title: Uniform Three-Fold Product Expansion of Algebraic-Geometry Codes over a Fixed Field
authors: Cassie Ding, Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A collection of classical codes $C_1,\dots,C_m$ has product expansion if every low-weight word in the sum of their extensions to the product space can be written as a sum of words supported on few lines, each line being a codeword of the corresponding $C_i$. For $m=2$ product expansion is equivalent to robust testability of the tensor code, while for $m\ge 3$ it is strictly stronger; it is the hypothesis on the local codes behind recent constructions of good quantum LDPC codes, good quantum locally testable codes, and quantum codes with transversal non-Clifford gates. No explicit family over a fixed field was previously known to achieve constant rate, linear distance for both the code and its dual, and 3-fold product expansion at growing length.
  We prove that for the one-point evaluation codes $C_i$ of length $N_i=728\cdot27^{\,i-1}$ and pole order $\lfloor N_i/5\rfloor$ on the Garcia--Stichtenoth tower over $\mathbb{F}_{729}$, the triple $(C_i,C_i,C_i)$ has product expansion with a constant independent of $i$. The dual codes $C_i^\perp$ then form an explicit fixed-field family of rate tending to $109/130$ and relative distance at least $8/65$. The proof is geometric: we view the words of the sum code as arrays on the product of three copies of the $i$-th curve of the tower, where the parity checks are sections of a line bundle. An exact generation theorem describes the sum-code words supported on the grid footprint of a suitable divisor. A support-localisation argument then shows that every low-weight array lies on such a divisor, after deleting a small number of coordinates. We also give a sufficient criterion for three-fold product expansion in terms of degree and genus ratios, yielding explicit families over every non-prime finite field of order at least $512$. The principal conclusions have been formally verified in Lean 4.

title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
authors: Johannes Br\"ustle, Simone Di Gregorio, Federico Fusco, Stefano Leonardi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08173v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight.
  We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction.
  We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

title: NOMA Assisted Coordinated Beam Hopping for VLEO Satellite Communication Systems
authors: Jiayang Kang, Xinwei Yue, Xuyang Zhang, Tian Li, Peng Yang, Chunyu Pan, Shaoli Kang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.08174v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper investigates a non-orthogonal multiple access assisted coordinated beam hopping (NOMA-CBH) scheme in multidimensional very low Earth orbit (VLEO) satellite communication systems, where multiple satellites employ CBH and coordinated beams jointly serve ground users and a dedicated ground station (GS). To characterize the VLEO-specific propagation environment, we develop a channel model that incorporates atmospheric attenuation, Doppler effects, and pointing perturbations. Building upon this architecture and channel model, a low-complexity decoupled (LCD) algorithm is designed to optimize beam scheduling and power allocation. We further derive closed-form outage probability expressions for the ground users and the GS, perform asymptotic analysis to characterize their diversity orders, and evaluate the delay-limited throughput. Simulation results demonstrate that: i) The NOMA-CBH with LCD algorithm achieves an enhanced system sum rate relative to orthogonal multiple access with coordinated beam hopping (OMA-CBH); ii) Across the considered heterogeneous traffic-demand operating points, the NOMA-CBH scheme achieves higher aggregate delivered traffic than the benchmark schemes; and iii) The outage performance of NOMA-CBH is better than that of OMA-CBH.
